title: Bat Fatalities at Wind Farms in Northern Spain — Lessons to be Learned
abstract: I analysed bat fatalities reported from 56 wind farms in the La Rioja, Soria and Aragón regions of northern Spain. Post-construction monitoring surveys revealed 147 fatalities belonging to seven species of bats, namely Pipistrellus pipistrellus (59%), P. kuhlii (14%), Hypsugo savii (18%), Barbastella barbastellus, Nyctalus lasiopterus, N. leisleri and Tadarida teniotis (< 5% each). In the mostly low elevations sites in Aragon, fatalities occurred between March and December and peaked (76%) from July to October. In La Rioja and Soria, where wind farms mostly are located at higher elevations, fatalities occurred between May and October and without any obvious late summer peak. The reports reviewed here revealed many deficiencies in their protocols that prevent comparisons with other studies nationally and internationally. For example, only five reports (9%) accounted for searcher efficiency or carcass removal biases. Consequently, fatality estimates appeared to be negatively associated with the number of turbines in the wind farm and also with the monitoring frequency, so that fewer bats seem to be killed when the monitoring intervals were longer. This should be of considerable concern for environmental authorities in Spain and elsewhere. Despite rapid development of wind power facilities in Spain, the impact surveys that are carried out at present are clearly inadequate with respect to bats.

## Bat Fatalities at Wind Farms in Northern Spain — Lessons to be Learned

**Article** _in_ Acta Chiropterologica · June 2012 DOI: 10.3161/150811012X654402

CITATIONS 28

READS 1,146

**1 author:**

Alvaro Camiña ACRENASL

**42** PUBLICATIONS **290** CITATIONS

## **Bat fatalities at wind farms in northern Spain — lessons to be learned**

## ÁLVARO CAMINA

_Apartado de Correos 339, 28220 Majadahonda, Madrid, Spain Corresponding author: E-mail: acamia@acrenasl.eu_

I analysed bat fatalities reported from 56 wind farms in the La Rioja, Soria and Aragón regions of northern Spain. Post-construction monitoring surveys revealed 147 fatalities belonging to seven species of bats, namely _Pipistrellus pipistrellus_ (59%), _P. kuhlii_ (14%), _Hypsugo savii_ (18%), _Barbastella barbastellus_ , _Nyctalus lasiopterus_ , _N. leisleri_ and _Tadarida teniotis_ (< 5% each). In the mostly low elevations sites in Aragon, fatalities occurred between March and December and peaked (76%) from July to October. In La Rioja and Soria, where wind farms mostly are located at higher elevations, fatalities occurred between May and October and without any obvious late summer peak. The reports reviewed here revealed many deficiencies in their protocols that prevent comparisons with other studies nationally and internationally. For example, only five reports (9%) accounted for searcher efficiency or carcass removal biases. Consequently, fatality estimates appeared to be negatively associated with the number of turbines in the wind farm and also with the monitoring frequency, so that fewer bats seem to be killed when the monitoring intervals were longer. This should be of considerable concern for environmental authorities in Spain and elsewhere. Despite rapid development of wind power facilities in Spain, the impact surveys that are carried out at present are clearly inadequate with respect to bats.

_Key words_ : bats, environmental impacts, mortality, monitoring, shortfalls, Spain, wind farms

## INTRODUCTION

Wind farm development across Europe is growing rapidly in response to the need for lowered green house gas emissions (EWEA, 2008), and Spain is one of the leading countries in the world. There were 19,148 MW (18,115 turbines) in operation by 1st January 2010, and the national goal was to develop a total of 20,155 MW by the end of 2010 to comply with the objectives of the National Plan on Renewable Energies (Ministerio de Industria, Turismo y Comercio, 2005). In addition to these Nat ional objectives, each of the 17 Local Governments (Au to nomies) has defined regional benchmarks that are likely to double this figure.

Wind farms may affect biodiversity by causing direct mortality to birds and bats (Langston and Pullan, 2003; Percival, 2005). Fatalities of bats have been recorded at wind facilities in North America (Arnett _et al._ , 2007; Kunz _et al_ ., 2007), Australia (Hall and Richards, 1972) and Europe (Ahlén, 2002, 2003; Dürr and Bach, 2004; UNEP/Eurobats, 2005; Brinkmann _et al._ , 2006; Ry dell _et al._ , 2010 _a_ ). However, the effect of wind farms on bats has received little attention in Spain, although there are

two published papers (Alcalde, 2003; Al cal de and Sáenz, 2004).

The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) is the appropriate tool to evaluate the effect of plans and projects on the environment. Pre- and post- construction monitoring (BACI methodology) has been suggested as a proper way to measure such impacts. According to UE Directives (85/337/EEC amended by 97/11/EC, 2001/42/EC), all potential construction sites must be evaluated within the context of large-scale integral assessment frameworks (see Telle ría, 2009). Although considerable amount of data from existing wind farm monitoring in Spain exists, the information is largely found in ‘grey literature’ which is generally not available to the public or the scientific community. A peer-review of the existing information is required in order to provide for a better understanding of wind power impacts on biodiversity. Results from existing wind facilities could help to develop better monitoring measures by identifying patterns and information gaps (see Dürr and Bach, 2004 for studies in Germany).

In this paper I summarize bat mortality at wind turbines in the La Rioja, Soria and Aragón regions, northern Spain since the year 2000. The goals are: i)

to synthesize current information and discuss its limitations ii) to assess if the methods currently used in Spain are adequate, and iii) to provide estimates of bat fatality rates at wind turbines in northern Spain.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

At present (1st January 2010) the area comprising the La Rioja, Soria and Aragon regions (64,000 km[2] ) had 3,187 MW (3,267 turbines) of installed wind energy capacity (AEE, 2010; Fig. 1. Of these, data from 56 wind farms, together accounting for 2,555 MW or 80% of the total output in the three regions, were included in this review.

The Ebro River Valley extends NW-SE across the La Rioja and Aragón regions and includes lowlands (< 700 m a.s.l.) mainly used for wine yards, crops and fruit cultivations. Natural vegetation is almost absent in this area, with _Populus_ sp. plantations surrounding most water courses. The area is densely populated. South of Ebro River runs de Sistema Ibérico mountain range with peaks reaching up to 2,262 m a.s.l. This range divides the Ebro Valley from the Central Plateau ‘Meseta’. It is forested with naturally occurring oak _Quercus rotundifolia_ , _Q. faginea_ , _Q. pyrenaica_ and beech _Fagus sylvatica_ , and both naturally occurring and planted pines _Pinus silvestris_ . Part of the ridge is pasture, used by livestock, or shrubland dominated by _Retama_ and _Erica_ species. The Central plain is naturally a high elevation (1,000 m a.s.l.) steppe with some oak _Q. pyrenaica_ and juniper _Juniperus_ sp. and mostly covered by croplands and pine plantations.

Survey data for La Rioja were provided by Dirección General del Medio Natural del Gobierno de La Rioja (monitoring period 2002–2008, 10 wind farms), Junta de Castilla y León for Soria province (monitoring 2000–2008, 14 wind farms). Finally, the Aragonese Local Government provided us with several birds and bats monitoring reports for the 2000–2007 period (32 wind farms) located in Zaragoza, Huesca and Teruel provinces (all these unpublished reports are available on request from the author).

Public access to environmental data is regulated by the 2003/4/CE Directive from the European Parliament. This directive is applied in Spain by the National Law 27/2006 (Boletín Oficial del Estado, 2006). This legislation was used to access and summarize the information. Further data about altitude, topographical features and vegetation cover for each wind farm was taken from aerial photographs available from the SigPAC application from the Spanish Ministry for the Environment and Rural Affairs MARM (http://www.mapa.es/es/sig/pags/sigpac/ intro.htm). Information on land use was obtained from the same application. Wind resource areas were then classified as either forests, pastures or croplands. I also classified each area as flat low hill (FLH), ridge (RDG) or mountain (MNT). Technical data of the turbines and the nameplate capacity were taken either from the original reports, from the Spanish European Wind farms Association (AEE, 2010) or from the manufacturer’s home pages (Fig. 1)

The results presented in the original reports were entered into a database that also included land use, topography and altitude and also the total number of turbines and turbine tower height. In order to estimate effect of differences in sampling efforts, the number of visits per year was also included in the database. I also calculated the fatality rates per megawatt and

per 2,000 m[2 ] of rotor swept-area (Arnett _et al_ ., 2007). The last two metrics allow for comparison among facilities of different power output.

Monitoring plans differ for each of the three provinces. Generally, the requirements on the duration of the monitoring are three years for Aragón, five years for La Rioja and the entire life span of the wind farm in Soria. Within a year, the search intervals varied between seven (during bird migration in Feb ru - ary–May and August–October) and 15 days, with a few surveys made on a monthly basis. Statistical procedures that I used included non-parametric tests and Spearman’s correlations. Cal - culations were made using STATISTICA 6.0 (StatSoft, 1997) package.

## RESULTS

Wind turbines in Soria were located at higher elevations on average (1,460 m a.s.l.) than those in La Rioja (1,034 m) and Aragón (580 m) [KruskalWallis (K-W) test, _P_ < 0.001]. In the former two regions the turbines were mainly located either in mountains or in forest and or pastureland while plains or small hills were mainly used in Aragón. Wind turbines used in La Rioja were on average taller than those in Soria and Aragón, respectively (K-W test, _P_ < 0.01).

Altogether, the 56 wind farms caused 1,662 fatalities, of which 147 (9%) involved bats. The bat fatalities were distributed among seven species: common pipistrelle _Pipistrellus pipistrellus_ ( _n_ = 68, 59% of the bat fatalities), Kuhl’s pipistrelle _P. kuhlii_ (16, 14%), Savi’s pipistrelle _Hypsugo savii_ (21, 18%), free-tailed bat _Tadarida teniotis_ (4, 3.5%), greater noctule _Nyctalus lasiopterus_ (5, 4.3%), Leis - ler’s noctule _N. leisleri_ (1, 0.9%) and barbastelle _Barbastella barbastellus_ (1, 0.9%). In addition, there were 31 fatalities (21%) that could not be identified to species. Sex and age of the dead bats were not provided in any of the reports (Fig. 2)

The overall pattern showed that the fatalities peaked in late summer and early fall; 87% of the dead bats were found between June and October. Distribution of fatalities extended from March to December in Aragón, but the fatality period started later (May) at the relatively high altitude sites in La Rioja and Soria.

The minimum (uncorrected) fatality rate at each site is shown in Table 1, and adjusted estimates are provided for five of these sites. In the latter five studies (9%), all conducted by the same team within a relatively homogenous area in Aragón, the observed fatalities were corrected for biases in detection efficiency and carcass removal rate. The detection efficiency was estimated to 36–40% and carcass removal to 8–13% between searches. The

All remaining reports give raw figures alone and without any corrections. For these (Table 1) the num ber of dead bats found per turbine per year (apparent fatality rate) was negatively correlated with the number of turbines in the farm (in Soria province only; _r_ s = -0.57, _P_ < 0.05 — Table 2). Furthermore, the apparent fatality rate was lower at sites where the sampling intervals were longer (K-W test, _P_ < 0.01 — Fig. 3).

## DISCUSSION

As far as I know this is the first review of the mortality of bats at wind resource areas in the Mediterranean region. Wind farms in northern Spain are built over a considerable range of landscapes including variation in topography and altitudes. The results of this review suggest that the mortality of bats at wind farms in Spain sometimes is very high. Nevertheless an overview of the gross results of the original reports without detailed analysis would have revealed a low impact of turbines on bats. This is an important issue for environmental managers at the Local Governments in Spain. Cur - rent monitoring programs clearly fail when assessing

the real impact of wind turbines on bats. The fact that mortality estimates seem to be affected by the number of turbines installed and the sampling effort (frequency of visits) shows that monitoring as currently employed is inadequate.

Most wind farms include more than 20 turbines (86%) and 26% have more than 40 (AEE, 2010), making proper monitoring surveys of the entire installations within a single day a very difficult task. Rioja monitoring are no longer carried out, because the respective three and five year surveillance programmes, as approved in Environmental Impact Statements, have ended.

In all the surveys reviewed, pre-construction information regarding bats use were missing principally because it was not required as part of the mon itoring procedures. In addition, the post-construction surveys were primarily designed for avian fatalities and with time elapsing between searching days based on bird phenology (breeding, migrating and wintering seasons); bats were not considered at this stage. As already mentioned, biases related to variations in searcher efficiency and carcass scavenging (Anderson _et al_ ., 1999; Morrison, 2002) may skew the results (Kerns _et al._ , 2005) and should therefore be accounted for. Close in monitoring shortfalls were detected in all studies relative to the recommendations given by Eurobats (Rodrigues _et al_ ., 2008) and there is yet no common monitoring protocol for the three regions or for the entire country. An agreement on a common monitoring method for bats and birds is extremely difficult in Spain as there are seventeen Local Governments each having different environmental policies, responsibilities and requisites.

The reported fatality rates are usually not true estimates and therefore cannot be compared with the result of other studies, whether these are made in Spain or in other countries. For the five wind farms for which corrected fatality estimates were provided, the results are comparable to those of some other studies although higher than in most. In fact the fatality rates in Spain are comparable to the highest estimates available from North America, namely Buf - falo Mountain in eastern USA (Fiedler _et al._ , 2007).

As in other cases, fatalities at wind farms in Spain are unevenly distributed among the species. Fernández Gutiérrez (2002), Alcalde _et al._ (2008), and Palomo _et al._ (2008) provided information on the bat species found dead at wind turbines in relation those that were known to be present. In Aragon, three of the 23 species present were found dead, five

of 26 in Soria and two of 22 in La Rioja. In the Navarre province, Alcalde (2003, in litt.) analyzed data from 1995 to 2002. Around 50 bats comprising seven species were reported. In addition to _P. pipi - strellus_ , _P. kuhlii_ , _H. savii_ and _N. lasiopterus_ he also found pygmy pipistrelles _P. pygmaeus_ , serotines _Eptesicus serotinus_ and common noctules _N. noctula_ . These species have in common that they normally forage in the open air sometimes above the tree canopies, and, therefore regularly move within the airspace occupied by wind turbine rotors (Rydell, 2010 _a_ , 2010 _b_ ). Lekuona (2001) studied six wind farms in Navarre. He detected 141 fatalities of which only three (2%) were bats (one _P. pipistrellus_ , one _H. sa vii_ and one unidentified specimen).

Despite the described monitoring shortfalls, the bat species found during the surveys are all considered widely distributed and abundant within the study area. There is no evidence of others with higher endangered status or significant population declines. Even a recent population increase has even been observed for _P. kuhlii_ (Palomo _et al._ , 2008). These species are considered as of least concern (LC) at the European level (IUCN, 2007). At the national level _N. lasiopterus_ is considered vulnerable (VU — Boletín Oficial del Estado, 2011). All bats are included in Annex II of the Bonn Convention, Annexes II and III of Bern Convention and Annex IV of EU Habitats and Species Directive. However, an analysis and a thorough review of the existing monitoring programmes is required in order to provide better under standing of the impact of already operating wind farms on bats. Results would help by identifying existing impacts or information gaps and to improve for better monitoring measures.
